segments.t: During a busy shift in the kitchen, molecular cuisine specialist Katya hurries over to Denis's station. She asked him to prepare simple watermelon pulp for a guest's order, but Denis has carved an elaborate surprise instead. Let's listen to their exchange in Russian.
Денис, я же срочно просила арбуз.
Мне нужна только мякоть арбуза.
Катюша, у меня всё уже готово.
Но достать её придётся тебе самой.
Тебе нужно победить эту акулу.
Ты зачем сделал эту акулу?
Слушай, Денис, люди ждут заказ.
Это же очень красивая акула.
Я хотел поднять тебе настроение.
У нас сейчас много работы.
Ладно, спасибо, ты мне поднял настроение.
Я сейчас быстро всё нарежу.
Now let's look at Katya and Denis's conversation over the watermelon carving line by line.
Денис, я же срочно просила арбуз.
'Denis, I urgently asked for watermelon.' Katya reminds Denis of her request using an emphatic particle, an adverb of urgency, and a feminine past verb.
Мне нужна только мякоть арбуза.
'I only need the watermelon pulp.' Russian expresses feelings and needs by saying 'to me it is needed' or 'to me it seems', putting the person in the 'to me' form.
Катюша, у меня всё уже готово.
'Katyusha, I have everything ready already.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
Но достать её придётся тебе самой.

'But you will have to get it out yourself.' Denis pairs 'to take out, to get, to reach' with 'it will be necessary' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
Тебе нужно победить эту акулу.
'You need to defeat this shark.' Russian expresses feelings and needs by saying 'to me it is needed' or 'to me it seems', putting the person in the 'to me' form.
Ты зачем сделал эту акулу?
'Why did you make this shark?' Here Katya anchors the thought on 'what for, why' and finishes on 'shark', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
Слушай, Денис, люди ждут заказ.
'Listen, Denis, people are waiting for the order.' In everyday Russian, 'listen' flows straight into 'order' without extra linking words.
Это же очень красивая акула.
'But it is a very beautiful shark.' Denis defends his handiwork with an emphatic particle and a feminine singular adjective.
Я хотел поднять тебе настроение.
'I wanted to lift your spirits.' Notice how Russian puts 'wanted' and 'mood' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
У нас сейчас много работы.
'We have a lot of work right now.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
Ладно, спасибо, ты мне поднял настроение.
'All right, thanks, you lifted my spirits.' Katya uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
Я сейчас быстро всё нарежу.

'I will slice everything up quickly right now.' Denis pairs 'right now' with 'will cut' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'. Let's hear their brief kitchen exchange again from beginning to end.

Katya is annoyed that customers are waiting for their order while Denis plays romantic games during work hours. Notice the nouns meaning watermelon, shark, and mood in their dialogue. Until next time!
До завтра!
